chapter: Vanguard and the Spirituals to Swing reissue
title: From Columbia to Dolly's Blue Eye label and Larry Welk's call about Vanguard
summary: After years as Columbia VP of A&R, Buckingham ran Dolly's Blue Eye imprint, grew restless, and was courted by Larry Welk to revive Vanguard on the Solomon brothers' model.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: That’s some nice behind-the-scenes info right there. So I’ve got three or four things I’d like to get through today. And before the cameras were rolling you actually answered one of my questions. And it was about the “Spirituals to Swing” re-issue. And I was wondering, this might sound snarky, but what made you think — my question was, what made you believe you are qualified to take on that project. But then you answered me with all the photographs you were talking about.

Well I’ll tell you how that all came about. I was with Columbia Records for ten, eleven, twelve years. VP of A&R. And then that was when CBS, Columbia and Epic, and I think it was around 1989 Sony bought Columbia and Epic from CBS. And I stayed on. And then — I can’t remember exactly the year, I want to say ’97, ’96, ’95, ’96, Sony approached Dolly about doing her own imprint (this will lead to “Spirituals to Swing” believe it or not), her own imprint label. And she called it Blue Eye Records. So the records from then on were Blue Eye/Sony. And that lasted two years and then we went to Universal. It was Blue Eye, Sony was on Sony of course, Tommy Mottola was the president then. Then we did it with Universal with Doug Morris. But about a year into it I told Dolly I said, “I just don’t think this is going to happen.” Because we were supposed to submit new acts to be signed. And they weren’t getting signed. And several of them went on to huge careers with other labels. So I was getting a little antsy I guess you’d say. And about that same time Larry Welk, Lawrence Welk’s son, started calling me. I was most of the time in Nashville but in L.A. a lot. They were in Santa Monica. Welk Music. And he started calling me. We knew each other, because he had Welk Music Publishing in Nashville and I knew — one of my best friends ran that. So Larry started calling me and said, “You know we’ve got the old Vanguard label we bought and we’ve been just kind of doing re-issues of the old Vanguard jazz series and those things. And we wanted to kind of re-vamp — “Ramp it up” he said. And he sounds the orders, “What would you do?” I said, “Well if it was me I’d do the same thing the Solomon Brothers did in the 50s when they started it in New York.” They signed artists, no matter what genre it was in — we were talking, I did a jazz class for Doc this morning and I was talking about the Solomon Brothers and starting Vanguard in the 50s in New York. Because they would sign Paul Robeson after he’d been blackballed in the red scare. And the Weavers after they had been blackballed in the red scare.
